extracted.intended_audience: jurors in patent infringement trials (and judges/attorneys using plain-English jury instructions)
extracted.subtask_description: Plain-English jury instructions explaining legal standards for patent infringement trials, including claim construction, types of claims, modes of infringement, novelty, and obviousness. Designed to guide jurors in applying the law to factual determinations about patent validity and infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Infringement (general definition and role of claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is infringed if someone makes, uses, offers to sell, sells, or imports what is covered by the patent, without permission. To figure out whether or not this patent has been infringed, you must rely on the patent claims. The claims define what the invention is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘Without permission’’ means without the patent owner’s permission or without other legal authority. The claims are the numbered paragraphs at the end of the patent and often are highly technical; the judge will tell you the proper meaning of the claim language, and it is your duty as jurors to accept that meaning. Claims are like a deed (they define the boundaries of property) or a recipe (apparatus claims = ingredients; method claims = instructions). According to the law, only the claims can be infringed; other parts of the patent application, such as the written description or drawings, are not bases for judging infringement. Each numbered claim must be considered one at a time; if even one claim is infringed, you must find in favor of the plaintiff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent and Independent Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two different kinds of claims: independent claims and dependent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent claims can stand alone; you do not have to read any other claim to know what an independent claim is about. Dependent claims do not stand alone; they refer to one or more other claims and incorporate whatever those claim(s) say. To understand a dependent claim you must read the dependent claim and the claim(s) it refers to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to Infringe a Patent (modes of infringement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law recognizes several ways to infringe a patent, including direct infringement, inducing infringement, and contributory infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Direct infringement: making, using, offering to sell, selling, or importing the patented invention. 2) Inducing infringement: intentionally inducing others to directly infringe a patent (called inducing infringement). 3) Contributory infringement: offering to sell or selling an item that is a significant part of the invention so that the buyer directly infringes; the offeror/seller must know the part is designed specifically for infringing the patented invention and is not a common object suitable for non-infringing uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (Newness / Prior Art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newness means that the invention, as it is, with all of its parts, cannot be found in any single piece of prior art. Prior art includes things, prior to the invention, that were publicly known, used in a publicly accessible way in this country, or patented or described in a publication in any country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a specific device already exists with all of the same parts as the patented invention, then the patent is not valid. Prior art is, by definition, publicly available; an inventor's ignorance of the prior art is not an excuse. For each numbered claim you must decide: Is the patent claim invalid because the invention was not new? If the claim's invention existed with all features in a single piece of prior art, find the claim invalid; otherwise it passes the newness test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness (Non-obviousness standard and factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is unpatentable if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made. A person of ordinary skill in the art is a hypothetical person who knows the prior art, has the relevant training in the field, and is not a genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To decide obviousness, jurors should: (1) consider the prior art and what was done before the invention; (2) identify similarities and differences between each claim and the prior art; and (3) describe the level of ordinary skill in the art at the time. Additional secondary considerations that tend to show non-obviousness include: commercial success of the invention; meeting a long-felt need; others' failed attempts to solve the problem; evidence that others took licenses and paid royalties; whereas contemporaneous independent inventions by others tend to support obviousness.
